analysis.one_liner: Restores federal pre-approval for voting changes in states with records of discrimination.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 218 cosponsors — every House Democrat — but never got a hearing, markup, or vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would rebuild the part of the Voting Rights Act that the Supreme Court emptied out in 2013: the rule requiring some states and counties to get federal approval before changing their election rules. It sets a new formula — jurisdictions with repeated voting-rights violations over the previous 25 years, or certain fast-changing demographics, must preclear changes like new ID requirements, cut polling places, or redistricting plans. It also requires public notice of voting changes and restores court standards for proving vote dilution.
analysis.who_benefits: Voters — especially Black, Latino, Asian American, Native, and language-minority voters — in states and counties with recent records of voting discrimination. They would get federal pre-approval screening before restrictive changes took effect, public notice of changes, and clearer court tools to challenge maps and rules that dilute their votes.

how_it_helps.text: States with 15 or more voting-rights violations in the previous 25 years (or 10 or more, at least one by the state itself, or 3 or more where the state runs the elections) would need Justice Department or court pre-approval for voting changes for 10 years; counties and subdivisions with 3 or more violations would be covered separately.

Even in uncovered states, specific practices would need pre-approval: new or tougher photo ID and proof-of-citizenship rules, cutting or moving polling places or reducing early-voting hours in heavily minority areas, certain redistricting changes, at-large election changes, and reductions in multilingual materials.

States would have to publicly announce voting-rule changes within 48 hours and post polling place resources — locations, machines, and poll workers — before federal elections, so voters are not surprised by last-minute changes.

The bill restores and updates the legal standard for proving vote dilution, lets courts consider a coalition of different minority groups as a protected class, and makes it easier to get early court relief against a voting rule adopted close to an election.
The Justice Department would gain authority to demand documents and written answers from states during voting-rights investigations, before filing suit.

analysis.who_pays: State and local election officials in covered jurisdictions, who would bear the cost and delay of submitting changes for federal approval and publishing detailed notices, and any state whose redistricting or election-rule changes would face a federal pre-approval gate.

drawbacks.text: The coverage formula keys off violations accumulated over the previous 25 years rather than current conduct, and in 2013 the Supreme Court struck down the prior formula on just that reasoning — that Congress was treating some states as more suspect than others based on old data — so this design would likely face the same constitutional challenge.

Covered jurisdictions would face real administrative cost and delay: every covered practice — including polling place changes and ID rules — could not be implemented until cleared by the Justice Department or a federal court, and smaller jurisdictions would have to post detailed public notices.

The bill gives the Attorney General broad new power to demand documents and sworn answers from state and local governments before any lawsuit is filed, which opponents view as an oversized federal role in how states run their own elections.
Preclearance decisions run through the Justice Department on a 60-day clock, so the protection's strength would depend heavily on which administration holds that office.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is large: it would put a federal checkpoint in front of election-rule changes in jurisdictions with recent records of discrimination, and require public notice of changes everywhere, which voters can actually use. The costs are real but narrower — administrative burden on election offices and a genuine constitutional risk, since the Supreme Court rejected the last coverage formula for resting on outdated evidence. The strongest honest objection is that Congress wrote the formula to survive that criticism but did not modernize it in a way the Court's current majority is likely to accept, meaning the bill might not survive a legal challenge even if enacted.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in September 2023 and referred to the House Judiciary Committee, which never held a markup or sent it to the floor, and it died there when the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Terri Sewell introduced the John R. Lewis Voting Rights Advancement Act of 2023 in the House on September 19, 2023.
It was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary the same day, and no further action — no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote — was ever taken.
The bill ended with 218 cosponsors, all of them House Democrats, and none from the Republican majority that controlled the chamber and its committee schedule.
The bill would restore a preclearance system under which covered states and counties must get Justice Department or court approval before changing voting practices.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Incumbent officeholders, state governments, and party organizations that prefer state-level control over election rules came out ahead: the pre-2013 status quo — no federal preclearance, and voting challenges handled case by case in court — stays in place. Because the Supreme Court struck down the old coverage formula in Shelby County v. Holder in 2013, there has been no pre-approval system since, and that remains the law.

for.name: Rep. Terri Sewell
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on September 19, 2023; it was referred to the House Judiciary Committee.

for.name: 218 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; the cosponsor list contained no Republicans.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee of referral; no chair scheduled a markup or hearing
against.what_they_did: Held the bill after referral; no markup, hearing, or committee vote appears in the action history through the end of the Congress.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.role: Majority party controlling the House floor calendar
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the floor for a vote during the 118th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 218 cosponsors were House Democrats and no Republican signed on; with Republicans holding 224 of 435 seats and controlling the committee and floor calendar, the bill had no path it could take without majority-party action.

industries.note: Covered jurisdictions would face new federal approval requirements, public notice deadlines, and potential document demands from the Justice Department, adding cost and delay. But where the underlying changes would burden minority voters, the bill's gate runs alongside those voters' interest in accessible elections.

The bill would put federal pre-approval in front of redistricting plans and election-rule changes — tools incumbents and parties use to shape the electorate — in jurisdictions with violation records. Its death leaves their current discretion intact.
The bill adds statutory causes of action, restores vote-dilution standards, eases early court relief, and authorizes attorney's fees, expanding the toolkit for groups litigating voting cases.
